live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: web skimmers that steal card details at online checkout
next.in_short: MageCart is a name for malicious JavaScript, and the groups that use it, that steals payment card data from online checkout pages. Reports describe attacks on single retailers and on shared platforms.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups use the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name several groups or clusters, including Magecart Groups 4, 8 and 12, Keeper, FIN6, Mirrorthief and ATMZOW.
eSentire says FIN7 is one of many cyber gangs observed taking part in Magecart attacks.
WIRED says Magecart has been behind some of the bigger hacks of recent years, from British Airways to Ticketmaster.
The main targets are e-commerce sites. WIRED says Magecart hackers cast the widest possible net to find vulnerable ones.
Malpedia's reference list also points to online ordering platforms and restaurants, with one headline citing 311 infected restaurants.
Trend Micro lists victims across retail, airline and ticketing brands, and online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.

ANY.RUN describes a campaign hitting mostly retail e-commerce sites, with victims in at least 12 countries and most in Spain, France and the United States. It says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
According to Malpedia, the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It copies data from input fields and sends it to command and control servers.
One report says most Magecart attacks begin when hackers use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.

Trend Micro describes infecting third-party firms that supply code to other sites, and scanning the internet for unsecured servers. It also describes writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.
Malwarebytes found Magecart-linked skimmers hosted on Heroku. The skimmers overlay a fake payment frame on the checkout form and send stolen data back in encoded form.
Sucuri describes the ATMZOW skimmer being planted through Google Tag Manager containers, with heavy obfuscation and many domains hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN describes checkout hijacking, imitation of payment pages and card data sent over WebSocket. It says the same injected code was also used to push an Android app.
RiskIQ reports a Magecart attack on Newegg. A lookalike domain was registered on August 13, 2018, and the skimmer was active around August 14. It was removed on September 18.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer code is recognisable from the British Airways incident.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months.

In October 2019, hackers breached the infrastructure of store provider Volusion. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher. It calls the incident a Magecart-style supply-chain attack.
ANY.RUN describes a campaign active for at least 24 months and supported by over 100 domains.
Sucuri says ATMZOW actors used 40 newly registered domains in late 2023. It says Google removed one container, and the actors created new ones and reinfected sites.
Merchants should treat unexpected scripts on payment pages as a sign of compromise and review any third-party code loaded at checkout.
